# VIA: VISUAL INTERFACE AGENT FOR ROBOT CONTROL

Hengyuan Hu, Jensen Gao, Priya Sundaresan, Satvik Sharma, Jeannette Bohg, Dorsa Sadigh Stanford University

## ABSTRACT

Robot manipulation is a complex task that requires visual perception, physical reasoning, planning, and closed-loop control. General-purpose foundation models (FMs) have grown remarkably capable of some of these, especially perception and reasoning. Inspired by the growing ability of FM-powered agents to operate software through visual interfaces, we ask whether that same competence suffices to control a robot directly given the right interface. We present VIA (Visual Interface Agent), a framework that recasts robot control as an agentic task where an off-the-shelf agent drives a manipulator directly through an interface. The interface is a virtual workspace of interactable visual components where the agent can probe pixels of interest with mouse-like tools and command a virtual endeffector to set new target poses with a small set of general tools. We show that VIA enables agents of varying capabilities to perform diverse tabletop manipulation tasks in simulation. We also use VIA to drive an off-the-shelf mobile manipulation robot in the real world to complete tasks that require both navigation and manipulation. Both settings are zero-shot, requiring no robot training or additional action primitives. Performance scales well with the size and strength of the underlying FMs. These results suggest that frontier agents already possess skills that transfer directly to robot control given the right interface: your coding or computer-use agent is, in a sense, secretly a robot-control agent.

## 1 INTRODUCTION

General robot manipulation is a long-standing research goal at the intersection of robotics and learning. It requires policies that are capable of complex visual understanding, physical reasoning, longterm planning, and precise closed-loop control. Foundation models (FMs) (Radford et al., 2019; Bommasani et al., 2021; OpenAI, 2023) trained on internet-scale data have become remarkably capable of several of these, such as visual perception and reasoning, which has made leveraging them for robotic manipulation highly attractive.

One approach for this is to convert existing vision-language models into vision-language-action (VLA) models, by fine-tuning them on robot data to produce low-level actions (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Black et al., 2025). However, due to a lack of both compute and robot-specific data, VLAs are often orders of magnitude smaller than frontier FMs. This gap has a profound impact on capabilities, particularly the physical reasoning and long-horizon planning skills that current robot policies lack.

Another paradigm is Code-as-Policies (CaP) (Liang et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2023), where FMs generate programs to control robots using perception APIs and hand-crafted skill primitives, e.g., mask = segment_text_prompt("green cube"), grasp_pose = sample_grasp_pose("red cube") (Fu et al., 2026). Although this is a natural way to tap into the strong coding capabilities of FMs, the FMs are not directly involved during rollouts. Therefore, the system is often bottlenecked by human-crafted perception and action abstractions rather than by the FM.

We propose a new way to connect FMs to robot manipulation: recasting robot control as a visual tool-use task for agents by introducing a virtual workspace that the agent can probe and interact with, similar to general computer use. Agents (Yao et al., 2023) wrap FMs with harnesses to enable better performance on long-horizon tasks (Yang et al., 2024; Jimenez et al., 2024), as well as closed-loop control of software or games in virtual environments (Anthropic, 2025a). They perform long-horizon tasks in a closed-loop manner, iteratively observing, planning, and executing, remarkably similar to what we want from robot policies. Therefore, we ask: given the right visual interface and human-legible tools, can a state-of-the-art agent control a robot without any robot-specific adaptation?

We present VIA (Visual Interface Agent), a framework for robot control that lets off-the-shelf visual agents drive robot manipulators through an interface (Fig. 1) and a controller. The interface is a virtual workspace where the agent interacts with the scene, staging and refining controller commands without affecting the real environment. The core component is a virtual target gripper that the agent can move around with a small set of human-legible Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (Anthropic, 2024b), much as a human would pose an object in 3D design software such as Blender. Through the interface, the agent reasons about the scene, issues MCP tool calls, and inspects their visual effects to refine the target gripper’s state until satisfied. The agent submits the refined target gripper state to the controller as a waypoint, and the controller moves the real gripper to that target. The agent then observes the updated scene and plans the next waypoint, repeating until the task is complete.

We evaluate VIA with two frontier agents, Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025b) and Codex (OpenAI, 2025a), across various model tiers. Our evaluation suite includes six simulated tabletop manipulation tasks and five real-world mobile manipulation tasks, spanning pick-and-place, articulated objects, precise execution, and long-horizon multi-object assembly. VIA achieves strong results, solving these tasks end-to-end in a zero-shot setting with high success rates at an estimated API cost of a few dollars per successful episode on most tasks. We show that VIA’s performance scales well with the underlying model capacity, achieving success rates of 38%, 73%, and 100% with Codex using Terra 5.6, Sol 5.6, and Astra 6, respectively, and showing a similar trend for Claude Code. VIA can also consume demonstrations written as plain text: providing a list of example waypoints increases VIA’s success rate with Claude Code from 62% to 76% and with Codex from 68% to 74% on simulated tasks. VIA opens up a new opportunity for leveraging state-of-the-art FMs at scale in robotics and demonstrates that, with the right interface, robot control can become another economically valuable agentic task that benefits directly from modern models and agents. Since VIA uses frontier models and agents unmodified, improvements in agent perception, reasoning, context management, and tool use transfer directly to robot control.

## 2 RELATED WORK

We review the following areas related to our work: existing ways to leverage FMs for robot manipulation, waypoint-based robot control, and computer-use agents.

2.1 FOUNDATION MODELS FOR ROBOT MANIPULATION

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. VLAs fine-tune vision-language models (VLMs) on robot data to directly predict low-level actions (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025). While these models have shown that FMs can enhance robot policies, their generalization abilities often still lag behind those of their base FMs, in part because fine-tuning on action data can degrade their reasoning and multimodal understanding abilities (Hancock et al., 2026).

FMs in Hierarchical Robot Control. Hierarchical approaches use FMs for high-level planning and reasoning while delegating low-level control to learned robot policies. SayCan (ichter et al., 2023) combines language-model planning with learned or scripted skill affordances to select which skill to execute. Text2Motion (Lin et al., 2023) extends this by verifying the geometric feasibility of the planned skill sequence with learned skill value functions. More recent approaches use VLMs to guide VLAs with subtask instructions (Shi et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026), 3D manipulation policies with predicted paths (Li et al., 2025), or diffusion policies with latent plans (Huang et al., 2025). FMs can also guide policy learning rather than execution: de Bakker et al. (2025) use VLM-generated keypoint trajectories as scaffolds and dense rewards to train a residual RL policy in simulation, so the VLM is no longer needed at test time.

Visual Prompting for Manipulation. PIVOT (Nasiriany et al., 2024) queries a VLM to select among visually annotated action candidates sampled from an iteratively refined Gaussian proposal distribution. MOKA (Fang et al., 2024) similarly prompts a VLM to select affordance keypoints and coarse waypoint parameters from marked images, relying on object segmentation, grasp proposals, and hand-designed motion routines to generate robot motion.

Code-as-Policies. Code-as-Policies (CaP) uses FMs to write code to control a robot (Liang et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2023). The generated code, rather than the FMs themselves, is the policy that handles perception and control. As a result, the code policies often rely on perception APIs like SAM-based segmentation and CLIP-based object retrieval to parse image observations, and rely on action primitives like grasping and placement modules (Liang et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023a;b) to handle actions. CaP-X (Fu et al., 2026) adds multi-turn execution feedback and allows the coding FMs to revise their generations after each attempt, but the policy still does not leverage the general power of the FMs during execution.

Comparison with VIA. VIA operates in a distinct setting different from the four categories listed above. Compared to VLAs, VIA uses off-the-shelf FMs and agents without any fine-tuning. In contrast to VLMs in hierarchical settings, VIA does not involve any low-level VLAs for translating instructions into robot actions. VIA allows agents to specify controller targets directly in the controller’s native degrees of freedom (DoF), avoiding any action abstractions or action-proposal primitives used in visual prompting. Finally, unlike CaP, which uses the generated program as the policy, the agent in VIA is the policy and remains in the control loop during execution.

2.2 WAYPOINT-BASED ROBOT CONTROL

Waypoint-based policies shorten the decision horizon by predicting sparse end-effector targets executed by a controller or motion planner (Shridhar et al., 2023; Goyal et al., 2023). HYDRA (Belkhale et al., 2023) and SPHINX (Sundaresan et al., 2025) combine waypoints for long-range motion with dense actions for precise manipulation. VIA builds on SPHINX’s visual teleoperation interface. Instead of having a human teleoperator collect data using this interface, VIA uses off-the-shelf FM agents to specify and refine waypoints to control the robot directly without robot-specific training.

2.3 COMPUTER-USE AGENTS

A rapidly growing line of work equips FMs to operate computer software directly through visual interfaces and a small set of generic tools (e.g., taking screenshots, clicking, typing) (Anthropic, 2024a; OpenAI, 2025b). Benchmarks such as OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024) and WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024) measure this competence on real desktop and web environments, and coding agents extend it to multi-step software tasks (Jimenez et al., 2024; Anthropic, 2025b). These agents exhibit strong closed-loop visual agency: they perceive an interface, act through tools, observe the outcome,

3 VIA: VISUAL INTERFACE AGENT FOR ROBOT CONTROL

VIA recasts robot control as an agentic observe-act loop over a visual interface. An agent operates a robot-control UI much as a person would: it takes a screenshot, reasons about what it sees, and issues intuitive commands through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools that stage a virtual target gripper visually representing the input to the controller. It then observes the result and adjusts until satisfied before invoking the controller to actually move the robot. It continues the loop until the task is complete or the episode times out. We describe the interface in Section 3.1 and the agentic loop in Section 3.2. The detailed list of MCP tools is provided in Appendix A.

3.1 VISUAL INTERFACE

The interface is a collection of interactive visual components that the agent can observe from and interact with. We first explain how the agents observe the world through the interface, and then how they control the robots by interacting with it.

All interface components are constructed from raw sensor inputs and robot proprioceptive information, without access to privileged state. When the depth readings are dense and reliable, such as in tabletop settings or in simulation, we reconstruct a 3D point cloud from RGB-D inputs and use it as the main workspace. When the depth readings are sparse, such as in our real-world experiments where a mobile base operates in a room, we simply show the 2D images. The 3D point cloud allows the user (either a human or an AI agent) to change the viewport by applying the orbit, pan, or zoom functions to a virtual camera, enabling views beyond those of the fixed cameras used to construct the point cloud. The agent observes this point cloud through snapshots of the current viewport, which it can modify, rather than the raw vectors of the points. The interface can be presented as a graphical user interface with a defined layout (as shown in the center of Fig. 1), or passed directly to the agent as a structured list of named, typed entries, such as JPEG image bytes and proprioceptive values.

An agent controls the robot by deciding inputs to the controller. For example, when controlling a single robot arm with a gripper, the controller inputs are 6-DoF target poses and a binary open/close state; when controlling an arm with a mobile base, the controller may additionally take 3-DoF base movement parameters. We refer to this set of target values as a waypoint. Instead of imagining and setting a precise target value directly given RGB-D inputs, the interface in VIA acts as a virtual workspace that allows the agent to probe and experiment with the target visually.

3.2 AGENTIC LOOP

An agent controlling a robot through a controller runs a simple loop: observe the scene, call the controller with a waypoint, observe the outcome, and repeat until a terminal condition is met. This closed-loop structure lets the agent recover from errors and re-plan based on what it observes, but the only feedback on a waypoint arrives after the robot has already moved, so every misjudged target costs a real motion.

With the interface, VIA keeps this outer loop but nests a mini-loop inside each iteration. Instead of committing a waypoint in one shot, the agent edits the target waypoint through any number of interface operations, each of which returns an updated rendering of the staged target on top of the real scene, and keeps revising until satisfied. Then the agent calls execute_waypoint, which invokes a controller that moves the real gripper to the target pose while obeying physical constraints. The mini-loop allows for trial-and-error to happen in the virtual workspace rather than on the physical robot: the agent verifies each waypoint visually before executing it, so the real robot only ever receives waypoints that have already been checked virtually. Fig. 3 shows one round of this loop, with VIA refining and then executing a single waypoint to prepare the gripper for opening a drawer.

We drive VIA using general-purpose agents, with no robot-specific fine-tuning or additional scaffolding, to demonstrate that, given the right interface and MCP tools, existing agents and models can be strong robot manipulators. VIA reuses off-the-shelf agents like Claude Code or Codex, including their tool-use loops and context management, so improvements in both the FM and the agent software can transfer to robot manipulation. We equip the agent with a short system prompt that covers the basics of the interface and provides general guidance on using it effectively, such as the configuration and limitations of the robot, the concept of waypoints and preference for closed-loop verification over open-loop execution (full prompt in Section E.1).

4.1 SIMULATION EXPERIMENTAL SETUP

Tasks. We use the following tasks in our evaluation (Fig. 4):

• Turn on stove: Turn on a stove by rotating its knob, from LIBERO-Goal (Liu et al., 2023). • Open drawer: Open the middle drawer of a three-drawer cabinet, from LIBERO-Goal. • Put bowl on plate: Pick up a bowl and place it on the center of the plate, from LIBERO-Goal. This demands reasoning on the grasp point and precision, as the bowl must be grasped by pinching its side wall and placed at the exact center of the plate to succeed. • Square: Pick up the square nut and fit it onto the square peg, from robosuite (Zhu et al., 2020). • Rainbow: Arrange seven randomly placed colored blocks into a rainbow, a task we created. This tests long-horizon planning and execution. • T-block: Build a T-shape with three blocks of the same size: one blue block on the bottom and two green blocks resting directly on top of it, side by side; from BuilderBench (Ghugare et al., 2025), re-implemented. This requires both solving a physics puzzle and precise manipulation.

These tasks test a diverse set of skills: manipulation, physical reasoning, long-term planning, and precise execution. All tasks run in the robosuite simulator. We use a simple PI (proportional-integral) controller that linearly interpolates between the current state and the target waypoint. The outcome of each task is a binary success or failure.

Evaluation Protocol and Baseline. We use Claude Code (CC) and Codex as our agents. To evaluate how VIA scales with the size and strength of the underlying model, we run CC with Sonnet 5, Opus 4.81, and Fable 5, and run Codex with Terra 5.6, Sol 5.6, and Astra 6. We run all agents at xhigh reasoning effort. On top of the shared system prompt in Section E.1, we give the model a simple task prompt by default, stating only the task description and success condition but no detailed instructions. We evaluate each agent-model configuration over 10 seeds per task, with varying initial object placements. We cap each episode at one hour of wall-clock time, except for Rainbow, which has a two-hour limit, although the agents complete most tasks in far less time when successful. We disable memory access for the agents so that they cannot accumulate experience across episodes. We also disable internet search and file access to prevent reading the exact task state specifications from the codebase2.

To isolate the benefit of VIA, we consider a naive baseline that uses the same inputs, agent, and controller setup as VIA but does not have access to the interface. It receives the same observations (snapshots of the same images and 3D point clouds, along with proprioceptive states) but must issue commands to the controller for immediate execution, without the ability to probe and iterate using any interface components.

VIA solves diverse manipulation tasks zero-shot. VIA achieves strong performance zero-shot in our simulation suite, achieving around 40% success even with the smaller models (Sonnet, Terra). The high success rates on Turn on stove and Open drawer indicate that VIA is able to handle articulated objects, beyond simple pick-and-place motions. The Rainbow task is specifically designed to test long-horizon planning and execution. We observe that the agents always plan carefully before moving any block, estimating each block’s location and choosing the ordering with the fewest moves. The effect of such planning is visible in their behavior: they sometimes assemble the rainbow with red on the left and sometimes with red on the right to minimize the number of motions required depending on the initial distribution of the blocks. T-block remains challenging for all except for Codex with Astra. All agents figure out the right strategy is to rotate the bottom blue block by 45 degrees to increase the contact area, but most of them fail to place the green blocks precisely on each half of the blue block, as this task tolerates only about 8 mm of placement error.

VIA scales with the capacity of the underlying models. Fig. 5 shows that VIA benefits directly from the scale of the underlying models. Performance of VIA improves from 43% to 85% by switching to bigger models in Claude Code and from 38% to a perfect 100% for Codex.

4.3 REAL-WORLD EVALUATION

For the real robot experiments, instead of staying in the stationary tabletop domain, we use a mobile manipulator, Stretch 4 (illustrations and details in Section D), that operates at room scale to demonstrate that the system works with coarse and noisy depth perception. The mobile robot also allows for a much wider range of random initial conditions, as well as multi-step tasks that require the agent to remember objects that go out of sight as it moves the robot. Unlike in simulation, where we have perfect depth information to construct dense, informative point clouds, the Stretch 4 robot has a head-mounted lidar sensor that provides depth information only for sparse points

We run Fast-FoundationStereo (Wen et al., 2026) for the stereo camera on the wrist to provide better depth estimation in the wrist view.

Tasks. We use the following tasks in our real-world evaluation (Fig. 6). Apart from the task-specific randomization described below, the initial location of the robot is also randomized.

• Lamp: Turn on the lamp by pulling the small chain downward. The lamp may not appear in the initial view of the robot. The chain is small and requires precise motion. • Shelf: Open the top drawer and put the toy lion from the shelf into the drawer. The toy lion’s location and pose are randomized over the shelf. The toy and drawer are far apart so that they do not appear in the robot’s view at the same time. • Towel: Fold a towel diagonally by bringing one corner to the opposite corner. The location and pose of both the towel and the table are randomized. This tests deformable object manipulation. • Wipe: Pull a wipe out of its container and use it to clean the black mark on the table. The location and shape of the black mark, as well as the location and orientation of the table, are randomized. • Basket: Open the basket until the lid flips to the back of the basket. The location and orientation of the basket are randomized. This manipulation of an articulated object requires complex motion.

Results. Table 3 summarizes the results. We evaluate VIA with Codex Astra 6 as the agent for five episodes in each task, and it achieves a near-perfect 24/25 (96%) success rate. These results show that VIA extends to real-world manipulation with commercial hardware. The Towel and Wipe tasks extend the evaluation suite to deformable objects. Apart from the quantitative results, these evaluations also exhibit several interesting behaviors. In Lamp, the task description mentions that the lamp is on a cabinet, and the agent is able to search for the lamp quickly once the cabinet appears in its view. The one failure in this task is when the agent overextends the gripper to hold the stem of the lamp instead of the chain, which could be a perception problem as the chain and the stem are the same silver color. In Shelf, the head camera’s limited field of view requires the agent to remember the locations of the lion and drawer to move efficiently between them. VIA does this using the underlying agent’s built-in context management, without any additional engineering. In Towel, the agent is able to fold the towel precisely so that the edges align well. In Wipe, the agent’s view is blocked when wiping, and it automatically moves the gripper away after a few wipes to check the cleanliness of the table. In one episode, it drops the wipe on the table and pushes it with a closed gripper instead of holding it, after the latter strategy fails to wipe cleanly. Finally, in Basket, the agent automatically retries within episodes when the lid slips out of the gripper during opening.

## 5 CONCLUSION

We present VIA, a framework that recasts robot control as a visual agentic task: an off-the-shelf FM-powered agent operates an interface built from RGB-D streams, posing target grippers and executing waypoints through human-legible MCP tools. Using off-the-shelf frontier agents, VIA solves six simulated manipulation tasks and succeeds in 24/25 trials across five real-world mobile manipulation tasks, without robot-specific fine-tuning or privileged state. Performance improves with model strength: each new generation of general capability transfers to the robot, with no fine-tuning required. One direction for future work is to include a more sophisticated controller, which could allow the system to avoid collisions or handle dynamic tasks. Another direction is to study how to extend similar ideas to dexterous manipulation beyond parallel grippers. Even in its current form, however, VIA has practical uses: assembly tasks where reliability matters more than speed, reset mechanisms for real-world reinforcement learning, and data collection in which a slow interface agent generates demonstrations for training fast policies.

Limitations. VIA achieves high success rates with the frontier agents, but inference remains slow and expensive. We expect similar performance from smaller and cheaper models as FMs continue to improve, with open-weight or less congested models further reducing cost and latency. Slow inference also restricts VIA to quasi-static tasks: it is not suitable for dynamic tasks like catching a ball. However, a wide range of quasi-static tasks carry significant value and existing methods are not yet reliable on them, making VIA a compelling option in this regime.

*Table 4: MCP tools for simulation. The agent perceives the interface with screenshot and poses the blue target gripper with intuitive tools such as gripper_teleport_via_click, gripper_translate, and gripper_rotate. It can also move the camera via the camera tools to disambiguate the scene. execute_waypoint moves the real gripper to the target pose through a controller. Most tools return an updated screenshot reflecting their effect on the UI or the real environment.*

The UI described in Section 3.1 already enables a human to control the robot. To make it operable by agents, we wrap its core interactions into a small set of MCP tools, summarized in Table 4 and documented in full below. The tools fall into four categories. Observation tools gather information about the environment. screenshot returns a screenshot of the entire UI. gripper_get_pose and camera_get_pose return the pose of the virtual target gripper that the agent is commanding and the current viewport parameters, respectively. We also provide two helper tools. hover takes a pair of normalized screenshot coordinates (u, v) and returns a screenshot with a virtual crosshair overlaid at that location, along with the 3D coordinates of the point it hits in the point cloud, if any. The agent can use it to verify that a planned click will land at the intended location, or to read off the 3D coordinates of points of interest. gripper_show_rotation_gizmo overlays a rotation gizmo on the target gripper to help the agent reason about rotation directions. Action tools manipulate the target gripper. They have no effect on the real robot until execute_waypoint is called. Each action tool returns a screenshot after its change to the target gripper is rendered on the UI, so the agent can check the outcome and keep adjusting until the waypoint is ready for execution. Camera tools change the viewport so that the agent can observe the scene from angles beyond the default view. Execution tools affect the underlying environment, either moving the robot via execute_waypoint, or terminating the episode via end_episode.

We design the tools around two principles: minimalism and agent ergonomics. For minimalism, each tool wraps the corresponding human operation with little or no extra abstraction, so agents can operate the system with the same control and freedom as a human. For agent ergonomics, we account for the fact that agents observe the UI through discrete screenshots rather than continuous animation. Operations such as rotating the gripper by dragging a gizmo axis or orbiting the camera with a continuous drag are therefore hard for an agent to comprehend, so we provide more direct alternatives, such as gripper_rotate and camera_orbit_via_key, which take exact angles as input.

gripper_teleport_via_click(u, v)

camera_orbit_via_key(d_azimuth, d_elevation)

Orbit the camera around the scene target by an angular delta, in degrees; returns a screenshot. You specify the two orbit angles directly, with no start point or open-space click needed, so it is the simplest way to reframe. Both deltas are relative to the current pose (read camera_get_pose for the absolute angles); the distance and look-at target are unchanged, as this only rotates the viewpoint. Positive d_azimuth swings the camera counterclockwise seen from above, negative swings it clockwise; at the default view, azimuth is 90 with the camera at Y = 0 looking toward −X, and positive deltas swing it toward +Y , reaching a view toward −Y at azimuth 180. A.1.4 EXECUTION TOOLS

execute_waypoint()

Execute the current gripper target and record one waypoint; returns a screenshot. This asks the robot controller to move the real gripper to the current target pose: position, orientation, and final open/closed gripper state. Use this after meaningful target-setting operations such as gripper_teleport_via_click, gripper_drag, gripper_advance_or_retreat, gripper_rotate, or gripper_toggle. Execute a gripper_toggle on its own; do not combine it with a pose change in the same waypoint, since moving and opening/closing the gripper at once is unreliable. Execution uses the final target as the next base state for later operations. The controller interpolates between the current pose and the target pose; it does not replay the exact UI trajectory used to place the target. For example, if you toggled the gripper twice before executing, it only tries to match the final open/closed state, without intermediate toggles. If this waypoint achieves the task goal, the result reports TASK SUCCEEDED and that the connection is about to close. When you see that, stop: the episode is done and no further tools should be called.

end_episode()

Save and end the current episode and reset or advance the task; returns a screenshot. Call this only after the final waypoint for the episode has been executed.
